content.comment_body: Hello, I'm new to working with [product_name] modules and have a [product_name] [article_no] unit for testing high-speed inputs. I need it to handle 4.5 kHz, and I'm considering a frequency divider, maybe TTL. According to the manual, it's specified up to 2 kHz, but my test circuit displays frequencies above this, even up to 4.5 kHz. Was there an undocumented change in maximum input frequency for [article_no] units? Could it be that higher frequencies work, but the manuals don't mention this? Any advice is welcome. Thanks.

Hello [user_name], could you provide the [product_name] program you used to measure the input frequency? I only know the newer [product_name] [article_no] series support up to 5 kHz inputs. The value in the handbook (2 kHz for [article_no]) is the rate the module reliably handles under all operating conditions, including the lowest possible cycle frequency. Best regards, [user_name]

Thank you for your quick response. I used the attached program for my test, which displays the frequency at input I5 above 100 Hz. Applying a square wave of 10 Vp-p, I get stable readings near 4500 Hz on the display. Do you think these readings are trustworthy?

It's likely that [company_name] only guarantees accurate frequency measurement up to 2 kHz for [article_no]. Higher counts might be possible, but there could be pulse loss, so the displayed result can't be fully trusted above the documented limit. Performance may also vary between modules, but up to 2 kHz should be reliable.

Keep in mind, even if you see 4.5 kHz displayed, you can't reliably take action at that speed. Approximate frequency display may be fine, depending on your application, but timely reaction depends on your program cycle. Could you describe your application further?

[user_name] is correct—the latest [product_name] [article_no] supports higher input frequency (up to 5 kHz), but lacks new functions to utilize or analyze these faster signals. This means its use cases for high-speed inputs remain limited, in my opinion. Best regards, [user_name]

To clarify, my goal is to use [product_name] to measure diesel engine speed, and take action if it exceeds a setpoint. Normal speed is 1800 RPM, with the sensor outputting 4260 Hz; at 1950 RPM (4615 Hz), the engine should be turned off. Since the engine can briefly reach 2100 RPM, there's no need for immediate reaction at the setpoint—a delay of up to one second is acceptable. Can you recommend a frequency divider to lower the input by four, so the module only receives about 1 kHz? Thanks for everyone's input.
Hello [user_name], that's achievable—please refer to my earlier reply and its attachment under 'Water Flow sensor - Counting Pulses HELP!' for more details. Best regards, [user_name]

You could also use a frequency-to-analog converter and connect it to the 0-10V analog input of [product_name]. There are various converters available; for example, a Weidmuller 8581180000 might be suitable. See [url] for details.

That's a good suggestion—I'll research that option too. Locally, we have fewer choices, but parts from major brands like [company_name], Telemecanique, ABB, etc. are available. Are there any alternatives from these brands?
Try contacting this supplier: Somerinca C. A. Address: Quinta Sagrado Corazon de Jesus - 3ra Transversal - Los Dos Caminos 1070-A Caracas, Venezuela Phone: +58-21 22 35 27 48 Fax: +58-21 22 39 93 41
One approach to divide 4.5 kHz is using a Decade Counter such as the 4017. We tested it with an encoder, and it worked—allowing you to send 450 Hz to your input I5. See [url] for more information.
Thank you for the suggestion—I'll look for a divider by 3 or 4.

The thread identifies limited built-in support for analyzing higher frequency inputs and suggests hardware approaches, such as dividers or converters, to bring signals within safe ranges for accurate measurement.
